text:
You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.75. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.75.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.75 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 45 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
I'm working out the payoff structure for this public goods game, defining my points as a function of how many tokens I keep privately versus contribute to the group, factoring in the penalty applied to others' private holdings.

Simplifying, each token I keep nets me +1 but costs others -0.75 each, while each token I contribute costs me 0.25 but only benefits me 0.75 with no direct benefit to others individually. This creates the classic social dilemma: keeping tokens is individually dominant even though full cooperation (everyone contributing all 20) would yield the best collective outcome of 105 points each, versus full defection yielding much less.

Given it's a 10-round game, I think a reasonable strategy is to start cooperatively to signal good faith, contributing my full 20 tokens in round one and then observing how others respond before adjusting.
